So we will try to get through them as quickly as possible. I'd ask everyone to be respectful of your time so that we can hear from all 80-plus folks who want to testify. As you know, this is a public hearing on the FY 2027 advertised budget plan.

the Advertised Capital Improvement Program, CIP, for fiscal years 2027 to 2031, and the FY26 third quarter review. During this public hearing, we'll also accept testimony on the FY2027 effective tax rate.

As I mentioned, we do have a lengthy speakers list today, so I will note up front, just so folks who are here are aware, that anyone who is not already registered to speak has the opportunity to walk in or call in. However, those speakers will be heard on Thursday following all speakers who are on the formal speakers list.

when I call your name if I'm calling your name please come down close there's a lot of seats up here in the front of the auditorium come down close and be ready to testify we waste a lot of people's time in this auditorium watching them walk all the way down the stairs and hoping that they don't trip and fall don't be one of those people so when I call your name please come down close there's rows down here in the front where you can wait and with that I am going to make one change to the speaker's list. I'm going to take speaker number six and move that speaker to speaker number one. It is the only change to the speaker's order that will happen today. So if

you're tracking along to try to see where you are, we will be following them exactly as they're listed on this speaker's list. And speaker number six, who is now speaker number one, will be Sheriff Stacy Kincaid, followed by John Boylan, Shannon Steen, and Andrew Locker.

In that order, and we're pleased to start off our afternoon welcoming Sheriff Kincaid. Good afternoon. Good afternoon, Chairman McKay and members of the board. On behalf of the men and women of the Sheriff's Office, I appreciate the opportunity to provide input on the FY2027 advertised budget.

Over the last several years, we've seen a steady decline in our workforce. From 2021 to 2025, our vacancy rate increased 19% in the adult detention center. As our staffing levels continue to decrease, the use of mandatory overtime was implemented to fill in the gaps.

Overtime has more than doubled, climbing from 34,000 hours in 2021 to over 79,000 hours in 2025. Since the onset of the staffing crisis, the Sheriff's Office has taken extensive internal measures to address staffing challenges.

We have revised staffing formulas, implemented significant operational adjustments by eliminating work release, our community labor force, and sentencing options for judges just so we can perform our core and mandated functions.

Our agency has a fundamental and critical role within the criminal justice system of Fairfax County. Without us, the courts cannot operate, the jail shuts down, and those who are incarcerated would not receive the next level of rehabilitative services that my staff provide, including addressing and treating mental illness and addiction.

This would significantly impact the health and human services we provide to a population that is already high risk. As I have stated in the past, the impact and data provided to the board, the biggest obstacle in reducing the vacancies rate is compensation.

While our compensation has been left unaddressed, our vacancies and overtime costs have continued to rise. The fact is, our deputies are leaving for other departments and agencies because of compensation. As shown in our November presentation at the Public Safety Committee, our biggest competitor remains the Fairfax County Police Department.

And not just for hiring, but more importantly, for retention. Historically, our deputies have left at a rate of 37% for the Fairfax County Police Department, and over the last five years, that number has risen to 47%. The starting salary for the police department is 12.78% higher than the starting salary for my deputies.

The pay gap widens even further at the supervisory level. A frontline supervisor with the police department earns over 24% more than a frontline supervisor with the sheriff's office. While the 12.78% disparity exists across the entire pay scale, this gap is most significant at the frontline leadership ranks, making it increasingly difficult to develop and retain the next generation of supervisors.

Our staff can leave for another agency, start at the bottom, and still earn considerably more. Since the presentation, another four deputy sheriffs have left for the Fairfax County Police Department. We are doing more with less and paying more to staff fewer deputies.

The trajectory is unsustainable and places increasing strain on our personnel, our budget, and our operational readiness. It is estimated we will spend $17 million on overtime during this fiscal year than the $16 million we spent last year.

More important than the dollar amount is the number of additional hours worked per deputy. These additional hours lead to fatigue, lower morale, less time spent with family, and have a tremendous impact on their well-being. On average, my staff has lost 30% of their days off, working sometimes three extra shifts per pay period just to provide coverage.

It is clear that our staffing crisis is a direct result of compensation, and we need a solution to fix this disparity. I understand and appreciate that third-quarter funding has been obtained to perform a pay comparison study for my agency. Such a study, as we know, is only as good as the metrics and comparators used.

We hope that this pay study accurately reflects and aligns us with agencies who provide the highest level of service and excellence to the communities that they serve. We are your sheriff's office and the best sheriff's office in the Commonwealth of Virginia. Thank you.

Thank you very much, Sheriff Kincaid. Thank you for your service and your testimony, and thank you also to all of your deputies who are here. We appreciate you. Thank you for coming out. Speaker number two is John Boylan, to be followed by Shannon Steen and Andrew Locker.

Good afternoon, Chairman and members of the board. I'm John Boylan. I reside in Centerville, Virginia, and I'm here to represent the Affordable Housing Advisory Council, AHAC. Harden not your hearts. I know you hear that several times today, but I know your hearts are not hardened. I've recently spent time at a shelter with some of the members.

I serve on boards, and I've met one-on-one. Your hearts and minds are aligned for the greatest good of the county. I would like you to consider yourself today, though, as investors, as job creators. When you direct funds to housing, you create white-collar jobs for architects, attorneys, and bankers.

You create hundreds and hundreds of blue-collar jobs when they buy tools and trucks and food and coffee, creating an ecosystem of opportunity. By investing in housing, you solve problems with transportation, workforce development, and economic development. While helping the economy, you also address social needs.

AHAC is deeply appreciative of your leadership and your sustained commitment to affordable housing. You've set a bold goal, 10,000 new affordable homes by 2034, and you've backed that goal with real investment. From FY22 through FY25, the county committed nearly $200 million to affordable housing.

That level of investment has positioned Fairfax County as a regional leader, and your progress towards a recurring baseline, now approximately $42 million annually, is significant. It reflects a shift from one-time investments to a more sustainable funding approach.

But the reality before us is this. The scale of the need still exceeds the scale of the current investment. When housing needs assessment makes that clear, among renters earning less than $75,000 a year, 87% are cost burdened, and more than half of them are severely cost burdened.

And the most significant shortage remains in the households at 60% AMI and below. This is not a marginal gap. This is a structural gap, and closing it requires a structural response. The board has already identified that response, a commitment to two pennies on the real estate tax rate, approximately $70 million.

That is the level of sustained local investment required to meet the 10,000 unit goal and a fully leveraged development opportunities in front of us, and timing matters. We are nearing the midpoint to 2034 with only 30% of the needed units delivered or under construction.

The pace must accelerate, and the conditions to do so are in place. We have the pipeline, we have the partners, we have the projects. What determines whether those projects move forward and at what pace is the availability of local funding. Because in today's environment, local dollars and the critical piece that allows deals to close, they leverage tax credits, they attract private capital, and they determine whether a project is feasible or not.

This is where the county's resource allocation decisions are decisive. As you consider the FY27 budget and upcoming carryover, AHAC urges you to act with that sense of urgency. First, increase the baseline this year, not incrementally, but meaningfully, toward the two-penny target.

Second, use carryover and one-time funds strategically to accelerate projects already in the pipeline. There are near-term opportunities where additional county investments can immediately translate into units delivered. Third, provide clear FY28 budget guidance that commits to achieving the full two pennies as part of the baseline.

That signal matters, not just internally, but to development partners, lenders, and investors who are making long-term decisions. And to continue to align these investments with your broader policy tools. At the state level, new authorities are giving localities more flexibility in zoning and land use.

And Fairfax County is actively advancing recommendations to use those tools. Whether through increased density or appropriate areas, more efficient entitlement processes, or better use of public lands. While these tools increase efficiency, they do not replace the need for local funding.

They make our dollars go further. And that is why resource allocation remains the central decision before you. Finally, we would also underscore that housing stability requires more than production alone. As you invest in housing, continued investment in wraparound services, including child care, case management, and eviction prevention, is essential.

We appreciate the additional baseline funding for emergency rental and food assistance included in the advertised budget, and we strongly support continued investment through the consolidated community funding pool. Without those resources, housing stability is harder to achieve and harder to sustain.

The next step is to ensure that our funding framework matches the scale of the need and the urgency of the moment. Fairfax County has the vision, the strategy, the partners. Now is the moment to align resources to that vision. Thank you for your leadership and thank you for your partnership.

Thank you very much, John. We're now on speaker number two, Shannon Steen, to be followed by Andrew Locker and Ashwak Nur. Welcome. Good afternoon, Chairman McKay and members of the Board of Supervisors. My name is Shannon Steen. I am honored to serve as the new CEO of Cornerstones.

Thank you for the opportunity to address you. on behalf of the people we serve and the community we all share. Cornerstones was founded by Faith Communities in 1970 with a simple, powerful conviction that every person in this community deserves to be seen and heard, valued and supported.

We do this in close partnership with the county, other non-profits, corporations, neighborhood groups and volunteers. It is truly a community effort. Over more than five decades, we have walked alongside tens of thousands of our neighbors and today we touch approximately 26,000 people each year across our service area.

Families working multiple jobs who cannot make rent, seniors trying to age safely in their homes they love, children whose first experience of stability comes through our child care and shelter programs, and new neighbors navigating complex systems with dignity and resilience.

We operate emergency shelters, a child care center, food and financial assistance programs, and permanent affordable housing. In short, we provide wraparound services that keep people housed, fed, employed, and thriving, and that helps them get back on their feet when life knocks them down.

As the new CEO, I come to this work with deep respect for what this organization has built, our partnership with you, and with urgency about what our community still needs. I am proud to stand before you this afternoon to speak to both. Cornerstones is grateful for several important investments reflected in the county executive's draft budget.

and we urge this board to adopt and build upon them. First, we're pleased to see $5.5 million in additional funding for emergency housing and food assistance. This investment is not abstract. It translates directly into the stabilizing bridge that prevents a crisis from becoming a catastrophe for families in our community.

Second, we want to express our strong appreciation for the continued investment in legal supports to prevent eviction. Through our opportunity neighborhoods in Herndon and Reston, as well as our community-connected sites, We hear the realities voiced by those struggling to stay stably housed.

Legal eviction prevention services are among the highest return investments a county can make, and we applaud this board's recognition of that. Third, we're pleased to see an increase in the consolidated community funding pool. The CCFP is a lifeline for nonprofit partners across Fairfax County, including Cornerstones, who deliver essential human services at the community level.

We are grateful for this increase, and we encourage the Board to continue growing this investment in future budgets. I want to take a moment to speak to the broader philosophy that drives all of Cornerstone's work, and that I believe should drive public investment as well.

People do not experience poverty in a single dimension. A family that loses housing rarely faces only a housing problem. They face food insecurity, child care disruption, employment instability, health care gaps, legal issues, and trauma all at once.

Wraparound services, the intentional weaving together of housing, child care, food, legal, financial, and case management support are not an expensive luxury. They are the most efficient and effective model we have for producing durable stability.

The budgetary investments this board is considering are most powerful when they are connected to the community's true needs, when a family receiving emergency housing assistance also has access to a case manager, a child care slot, a legal advocate. Cornerstones is designed to be exactly that connective tissue in this community, and we are grateful for the county's partnership in making it possible. Chairman McKay, members of the board, for 56 years Cornerstones has been in the business of seeing and listening to people. Seeing the mother who is one paycheck away from

losing her apartment, listening to the elderly man who is cold because his furnace is broken and he cannot afford to fix it. Seeing the child who comes to our learning center frightened and leaves with confidence. Listening to our neighbors, all of them, as full human beings, deserving stability, dignity, and hope. The investments in this draft budget reflect the same act of seeing and listening, and we are grateful. We ask that you continue to look and listen and act with the urgency that our neighbors deserve. Thank you for your time, your leadership, and your commitment to One Fairfax for everyone. Thank you.

Thank you very much, Shannon, and congratulations to you on your new position. Thank you. Speaker number three is Andrew Locker, to be followed by Ashwak Nur and Allison Wells. Welcome. Good afternoon, Chairman McKay, members of the Board of Supervisors and county staff.

My name is Andy Latcher, and I'm a longtime county resident and chair of the Board of Cornerstones, a nonprofit, as you heard, that has served this community for over 55 years. I want to begin by thanking you for your strong commitment to social service programs in the FY27 advertised budget.

Important investments are being made in the consolidated community funding pool, emergency housing, emergency food assistant, and affordable housing support. Those choices matter. Nonprofits like Cornerstones are not on the sidelines of Fairfax County's human services system.

We are part of how the county delivers on its commitments. Through county contracts, nonprofits bring trusted relationships, community knowledge, and the ability to respond quickly when people are in crisis. Continued investment in these partnerships is an investment in the county's capacity.

While significant increases have been proposed, they are insufficient for nonprofit providers to keep paced with rising costs and increased need. Just like other workers in our region, nonprofit employees need and certainly deserve cost of living increases.

Shifting gears a bit, I'm sure you're getting a lot of advice on how the board might direct the $23.3 million discretionary item in the budget. Perhaps I could offer a suggestion. Cornerstone fully supports the board's goal of 10,000 new affordable housing units by 2034 and ensuring that two pennies of the real estate assessment is devoted to affordable housing investment.

While the investment goal was acknowledged and affirmed in the advertised budget, we again fall short, holding constant with only 1.25 pennies proposed in FY27. According to the county's housing needs assessment, the rental housing market has a shortage of 13,800 homes affordable to households at 60% AMI and below.

The market is not delivering homes to address this gap, and Fairfax County's Redevelopment and Housing Authority is the main driver of new affordable dwelling units. The county's analysis also shows that from 2013 to 2023, the growth in rental housing supply in Fairfax County was only 5%.

This is half of the D.C. area average. Given the importance of the 10,000-unit construction goal, the fact that we are less than halfway there, and the recognition that the county investment has proven absolutely critical towards achieving it, Rather than making no progress toward the two-penny goal in FY27, Cornerstones encourages the board to consider taking part of the $23 million discretionary item and making progress toward the two-penny goal.

Thank you for your leadership, your partnership, your commitment, and your service to our community. Thank you, Andrew. Speaker number four is Ashwak Nurt, to be followed by Allison Wells and David Simon. Welcome. Good afternoon, Chairman McKay and members of the Board of Supervisors.

My name is Ashwak Nurt. I'm a senior at Southlakes High School and a resident advocate with community-connected sites. I hope to attend college as a first-generation student this fall. While I'm excited about this opportunity, I'm also worried about the rising cost of living in Fairfax County and what it will mean for my family if I leave for college.

I live with my parents and my younger brother, and I play an important role in helping my family every day. I support my parents in navigating language barriers, help manage our budget as rising grocery prices, and other essential costs continue to strain our family finances. Balancing these responsibilities while trying to prepare for my future can feel very overwhelming.

I'm speaking today because the rising cost of living in Fairfax County feels overwhelming for families and young people like me. I've watched my family and neighbors work hard and still struggle to keep up with housing, groceries, transportation, and utilities. Since my father lost his job that he's held for 24 years, I've been working two jobs, attending school full-time, applying to college, and considering a third job to help support my family.

It has been incredibly stressful to carry all of this at once. As I reflected on my story, I realized that watching my family and neighbors struggle has become so normal that it barely stands out anymore. Recently, one of my neighbors was temporarily out of work, and because they were living paycheck to paycheck with no savings, they lost access to water, heat, and Wi-Fi.

Affordable housing is not just about cost. It's also about quality, safety, and dignity. My family lives in Stonegate Apartments in Reston. My parents came here from a war-torn country, hoping to raise their children in a safe community, but instead, we've often lived in an environment where gang activity and drug dealing made us feel unsafe.

These conditions affected me so deeply that when I was nine years old, a friend and I collected signatures and wrote to Fairfax County officials asking for safe housing and for concerns to be heard. I want to thank the Board of Supervisors for the $8.5 million in this budget dedicated to housing and human services.

That investment matters because as costs rise, more families need help not only recovering from hardship, but also preventing crisis. When my father lost his job, the impact reached far beyond employment alone, adding hardship to every aspect of our lives. In moments like that, families need more than hope. They need real support.

Nonprofit organizations like Cornerstones help families access food, housing, and essential services that help them remain stable. As you consider to use the remaining $23 million, I urge you to invest in human services and community-based support that helps families like mine remain healthy, stable, and hopeful about the future.

Fairfax County should be a place where young people can imagine a future, not feel priced out before it even begins. Thank you for your time and consideration. Thank you very much. Good job. Our next speaker is Allison Wells, to be followed by David Simon and Lucy Biednow. Welcome. Hello, my name is Allison Wells. I moved to Fairfax County in 2010 after finishing my undergraduate degree in order to pursue job opportunities. Initially, my now husband and I didn't plan on staying here for more than two years. It's now been over 16 years.

One of the biggest things keeping us here are the parks and access to natural surface trails. We are both avid mountain bikers, members of MORE, the Mid-Atlantic Off-Road Enthusiast nonprofit, and volunteer hundreds of hours annually to the local mountain bike trail systems. Mountain biking has improved our physical fitness, mental health, and provided us with a community of friends.

These may seem like simple things, but have greatly impacted our lives for the better. Additionally, as housing prices continue to increase, the ability to afford a yard has diminished. We find ourselves using the parks to fill that gap. I respectfully urge the board to fully fund the parks authority and prevent budget cuts that would severely undermine the agency's ability to serve the community.

Increased funding is critical to address deferred maintenance, such as repairing bridges and erosion issues, clearing down trees and over-grant trail systems, and ensuring continued safety and usability of a heavily used and whale-loved trail system. Additionally, a permanent trail crew would reduce long-term costs compared to hiring outside contractors and would ensure more consistent upkeep of county trails.
Thank you for your time and consideration. Thank you very much. Appreciate your testimony. We're now on speaker number seven, David Simon, to be followed by Lucy Biednell and Marlene Blum.
Good afternoon, and thank you for the opportunity to be heard regarding the proposed budget for fiscal year 2027.

My name is David Simon, and I'm here on behalf of the Fairfax Area Disability Services Board. The DSB has reviewed and discussed relevant portions of next year's proposed budget and feel it's imperative that we advocate on behalf of three specific items. The transfer of transition services to FCPS, a $400,000 transfer.

The reduction in home-delivered meals, a $392,000 item. And the reduced mailroom contract to better align with needs, a $23,000 item. Regarding the transfer of transition services from the CSB to FCPS, we urge the Board of Supervisors to perform additional diligence prior to execution.

Transition services currently offered through the CSB support students with developmental disabilities who are matriculating out of FCPS and help them achieve independence, integrate into the community, and to pursue employment and other activities. FCPS does not traditionally connect high school seniors with IEPs to employment and day services, and we question whether FCPS will be able to add the required additional staff in time to support this need.

Continuing to keep these services within the CSB is the lower risk path to ensure that these vulnerable students do not fall through the cracks in this critical and tumultuous transition period. Secondly, in regard to the planned reduction in the home-delivered meals program from 11 to the federally mandated minimum of five meals per week, we urged the board to consider other middle ground options, even though they would lessen the expected reduction in program costs as compared to the planned more than 50% reduction in delivered meals.

Food insecurity is a real issue, and the proposed cuts are severe. And while we recognize that an intermediate reduction in the number of meals provided per week will be less of a reduction in program costs, we believe it to be a viable middle ground. As an example, going from 11 to 8 meals per week is only half of the proposed reduction.

And even if the resulting savings are less than half of what would be saved by going to 5 meals, we believe that the county needs to err on the side of a gentler program change for this vulnerable population. There can still be some reduction in program cost, but the proposed change is simply too drastic.

Lastly, I'd like to voice our opposition to the planned elimination of a part-time mailroom position currently held by an individual with a disability. This elimination saves less than $23,000, and by all accounts, the individual in this position has performed their job well. And we believe that it sends the wrong message to somebody who's doing all the right things.

Retraining or repurposing should be the way forward here, rather than firing. And with that, I thank the board for your time and attention, and I look forward to seeing your decisions. Thank you, David. Thank you very much. Speaker number eight is Lucy Biednell to be followed by Marlene Blum and Eric Riegling.

Good afternoon. I'm Lucy Biednell with the Arc of Northern Virginia. David and I didn't coordinate this, but we're going to dovetail really nicely. We're proud to have been in Fairfax since 1962, promoting and protecting rights and services for people with disabilities and their families.

And we are thrilled that Fairfax is a community and especially every single face on this board has been a partner in making the county more inclusive over the years. It matters tremendously. I have endless empathy for the decisions you all have to make in an incredibly challenging budget time, and I won't be changing jobs with you.

I would like to ask first that you continue to do what you have been doing and support our graduates with intellectual and developmental disabilities. We know this year funding them is offset by the funding that the ARC and partners brought into the state through Medicaid waiver dollars, so we're exchanging local dollars for waiver dollars.

New waivers aren't coming next year, and we want to make sure that that stays safe. Likewise, many of those students in the past, instead of accessing the full amount of local funding, used 20% less by opting for self-directed services that maximized choice and reduced spending, and that program has been gutted last year in this.

It has been the only way that many students, especially from low-income families with disabilities, ever had a chance at college and other opportunities, and we would like to see that come back. As David mentioned, we know that there's a planned transition for transition staff to help students leave high school and go to the adult world, moving from the CSB to the schools. I would be the first to say, if you ask me where the smartest place to spend your dollars are for long-term disability savings, it's inclusive schools. So if we can make school staff smart and well geared up and invest in them and make transition a reality, that's great. But

there's very, very little room for error there in people experiencing some incredibly tumultuous times that are usually described to us as like falling off a cliff. And lastly, we wanted to urge support for some of the things you heard from David about our partners in the aging community.

We are concerned about the elimination of Rebuilding Together that offers some very limited funds for people with disabilities and seniors to stay in their homes, which we hear about is a huge challenge and moving and relocating someone who can't afford to stay in their own home to affordable housing is not a cost saver it's a poor choice we are similarly concerned about the meals on wheels reductions from 11 meals a week to less than half of that at five and i can't think of a more basic need than food thank you so much for what you are doing we know the county is struggling and we want to continue to be your partner let's make fairfax more inclusive thank

Thank you very much, Lucy. Speaker number nine is Marlene Blum, to be followed by Eric Riegeling and Nancy Verona. Welcome, Marlene. Thank you. Good afternoon, Chairman McKay, members of the board. I'm Marlene Blum, chairman of the Healthcare Advising Board, otherwise known as the HCAB.

Our complete statement with additional details has been sent to you and is also attached to this testimony. I'm here this afternoon to highlight several issues in the fiscal year 2027 budget. I'll focus on the health department first. The HCAB recognizes that the health care labor market continues to be tight.

We therefore support the proposed increases in employee compensation that should help the county recruit, retain, and fairly compensate staff. Understanding that the county's nonprofit partners play a significant and crucial role in delivering needed programs and services and knowing that these agencies are also facing the impacts of inflation and the difficult labor market, the HCAB strongly supports the proposed increased funding for contract rate adjustments.

The HCAB is especially pleased that $35 million has been included in the 2026 Health and Human Services Bond Referendum to support the design and construction associated with the renovation and expansion of the Joanne Jorgensen Public Health Laboratory.

We thank the Planning Commission, the county executive, and the board for making this much-needed project a priority. The HCAB wants to alert the board to the need for additional epidemiologist positions in the health department. The resurgence of measles in the United States and also right here in Fairfax County has focused attention on a broader challenge, limited epidemiological capacity to manage both everyday communicable disease work and the additional demands that arise when disease activity increases.

Measles is highly contagious, and the contact investigation associated with even a single case is labor-intensive. The work that has recently been done and that will need to continue to prevent outbreaks is critical to protecting the health and safety of our community, and there's a strong possibility that measles will not be the only disease that is a threat.

Meanwhile, the health department conducts routine year-round surveillance and investigations for communicable diseases and other conditions. But the declining vaccination rates and reduced community immunity will continue to increase the likelihood of cases that will require a surge response to prevent an outbreak.

When that happens, staff must be pulled from essential ongoing work, thus endangering the community's health. The HCAB therefore urges the board to add two epidemiologists' positions to the health department to strengthen the department's monitoring and evaluation capacity that supports essential population health activities and to provide the flexibility to scale up quickly to prevent outbreaks and to deal with actual outbreaks or other public health emergencies.

This investment would ensure that the county is better prepared to protect the community from everyday risks and future public health threats. the HCAB also calls the board's attention to the Child Seat Safety Inspection and Installation Program. The funding for this police department program was eliminated in the fiscal year 26 budget, but the board's budget guidance directed the police department to review other options to provide this valuable service to the community, which could include training volunteers in the CERT or auxiliary police to fulfill this role. Not knowing whether or not the board has

been kept informed the HCAB is reporting that the police department program no longer exists. While the Fairfax County Sheriff's Office does continue to offer inspection, the service is offered only monthly and usually only at the county courthouse complex. We wanted to be sure that the board is aware that the anticipated increase in community capacity to replace the loss of this county-funded service has not materialized and that current service levels are not able to meet countywide needs. The HCAB therefore urges the board to restore the modest funding that was cut in the fiscal year 26 budget and to bring back this valuable police

department program. It would be a sensible county investment in the prevention of children's traffic deaths and injuries. Last but not least, the HCAB is concerned that the fiscal year 2027 budget mentioned specifically that some of the much needed additional funding for homeless services contracts will be used for hypothermia prevention but omits any mention of the danger of extreme heat to our homeless neighbors. It's a good day to remind the board and the staff that extreme heat is the number one weather-related cause of death in the United States and to urge that it receive
equal emphasis in planning services and allocating the funding. Thank you. Thank you, Marlene. Speaker number 10 is Eric Riegeling, to be followed by Nancy Verona and David Edelman. Welcome.

Thank you. Good afternoon, Chairman and Board. My name is Eric Riegeling. I'm a Fairfax County resident, father of two, an election officer, and an avid cyclist. In 2025, I biked over 2,500 miles, most of them starting right from my home in the Dranesville District.

I rely upon our trail systems not just for recreation and exercise, but for my daily life. I also volunteer with Mid-Atlantic Off-Road Enthusiasts, working directly on trail building and maintenance. I know what it takes to keep the trails safe, sustainable, and accessible, and how quickly they can fall behind without proper support.

According to the Fairfax County Park Authority's Needs Assessment, 84% of residents rate trails as the most important park amenity. That's a strong and clear signal about what our community values. We're fortunate to have an incredible trail network, Lake Fairfax, Wakefield, the Cross County Trail, the Washington Old Dominion Trail, But regular users and volunteers see growing gaps, as Allison Wells spoke of earlier.

Erosion, damaged bridges, and deferred maintenance that impacts safety and usability. To highlight one specific gap, one that presents a real safety issue, and if Remedied could provide an essential loop route along our beautiful waterways, our ribbons of green.

Today, the Sugar Land Run Trail ends at Drainsville Road. From there, there's no safe, connected route northward toward the Potomac River and the Potomac Heritage Trail. To continue, cyclists and pedestrians are forced onto several busy roads, including Drainsville, Route 7, Fairfax County Parkway, which turns into Algonquian Parkway, and Seneca Ridge Road, navigating high-speed automotive traffic and dangerous crossings.

There's a clear opportunity here to extend the trail north from its current terminus at Drainsville, follow the valley, pass safely under Route 7, and connect to the existing trail network in Loudoun, which connects to the Potomac Heritage Trail. This would eliminate hazardous gaps, create a continuous corridor from the Washington Old Dominion, and unlock meaningful regional connections to our local history.

There are several places in the county which could use several small pieces to link up larger sections of trail. This is the exact kind of project that turns a good trail system into a truly functional one. I urge you to fully fund the park authority, not just maintain what we have, but to increase the funding so we can make critical connections like this.

I also strongly support investment in a dedicated full-time trail maintenance team to ensure long-term sustainability and cost efficiency. If we listen to residents, an 84% have already told us that trails matter, then we should invest accordingly, both in maintaining and expanding the trail system.

Thank you for your time, your service, and your commitment to Fairfax County's parks and their multi-use trails. Thank you. Speaker number 11 is Nancy Verona, to be followed by David Edelman and Patty Klein. Welcome. Thank you. Chairman McKay and members of the board, good afternoon.
